title: Plan Lent
hookLine: one thing to give up, one to take up
tomorrow: after Easter Sunday, why keep celebrating for weeks?

lines: ONE THING OUT, ONE THING IN.
cards: Chocolate. Social media. The snooze button.
Those are the classic answers when someone asks what you're giving up for Lent. But a plan that only subtracts leaves a gap. What fills the space where the chocolate used to be?
Lent, at its best, is a trade: one thing out, one thing in.

teach.b: The question underneath: what is a season of going-without for? Lent is the season before Easter, and tradition ties it to Jesus in the wilderness, where Matthew says he fasted forty days and forty nights.
Some churches open it with ashes on Ash Wednesday; others mark it more quietly.
For the plan itself, Matthew 6 is the place to look: Jesus sets three practices side by side, giving, praying and fasting, and asks that each be kept between a person and God.

The prophet Joel says what all three are aiming at, in the King James Bible: “And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God.” Tearing your clothes was an outward sign of grief.
Joel asks for the inside to turn. So a Lent plan has two halves. Less: one thing set down.
More: one thing taken up. The less makes room; the more fills it. Now a neighbor.
Muslims fast in the month of Ramadan, and the Qur'an says fasting is prescribed for believers as it was prescribed for those before them, so that they may guard themselves against evil.
Shared ground: a season of fasting meant to turn a person toward God, a season the Qur'an itself says others kept before.
An honest difference: for Muslims, Ramadan's fast is commanded in the Qur'an, from first light until nightfall, all month.
For Christians, Lent is a church season, and churches keep it in different ways.

how: Christians keep Lent in different ways: some churches begin it with ashes on Ash Wednesday, and some people give something up and take a practice up, drawing on the giving, praying and fasting of Matthew 6.

o: a vow made once, on Ash Wednesday, for life
choosing one thing to give up and one to take up
a list of foods that are banned until Easter

games.q: less and more — tap the pairs.

s: Lent is only about giving something up
Matthew 6 sets giving and praying beside fasting: the less makes room, the more fills it.
the Qur'an says fasting was prescribed for people before Muslims too
Qur'an 2:183 says fasting is prescribed for believers as it was for those before them.
Joel asks people to tear their clothes to show they're sorry
the reverse: rend your heart, and not your garments.

games.q: your coworker gave up sugar for Lent and by week two she's miserable and snappy. what does Joel's line suggest she might be missing?
o: a "more" beside the less: a turned heart, not just a menu.
a stricter rule, so she stops slipping on the weekend.
permission to quit, since misery means it isn't working.
games.why: rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD. the going-without is meant to make room for something.

practice: Hold out both hands. Turn one palm down, as if setting something on a table, and name the one thing you'd put down for Lent.
Turn the other palm up, as if receiving, and name the one thing you'd take up: a gift, a prayer, a kindness. Hold both hands still until the sit ends.

wordCard.voice: Plan Lent. One thing to give up, one to take up, both aimed at a turned heart, and decided before the season starts.

orig.note: the Greek verb for 'to fast' in Matthew's Gospel.

carryVoice: Carry this: less and more, a palm down and a palm up. See you tomorrow.
